title: Broken Calculator
hints: going forward from startValue, doubling can wildly overshoot target, making the search space huge - what happens if you instead think about the operations in reverse, starting from target?
in reverse, 'subtract 1' becomes 'add 1', and 'double' becomes 'divide by 2' - but you can only reverse a double if the current number is even
when target is even, is there ever a reason to add 1 twice instead of just dividing by 2 once? dividing by 2 covers more ground in a single step, so whenever target is even, always prefer halving
when target is odd, you have no choice but to add 1 first (to make it even), since you can't reverse a double on an odd number

keep applying this (halve if even, else add 1) until target <= startValue, then the remaining gap is closed purely by 'subtract 1' operations in the forward direction, costing exactly startValue - target more steps - why is this final stretch always just a straight subtraction, with no more doubling useful? because once target has dropped to or below startValue, any further reverse-doubling would only make target smaller than necessary, forcing extra add-1 steps to compensate, which is never better than direct subtraction
commonMistakes: trying to greedily decide forward from startValue whether to double or subtract first, which doesn't have an obvious safe local rule the way the reverse direction does
continuing to divide by 2 in reverse even after target has dropped below startValue, instead of switching to plain subtraction for the remaining gap
not handling target < startValue specially, forgetting that doubling is never useful when you only need to decrease

content.problemStatement:
A broken calculator starts showing `startValue`. It supports exactly two operations: double the displayed number, or subtract 1 from it.

**Return the minimum number of operations needed to make the display show `target`.**
notes: target is smaller than startValue (only subtraction is ever useful)
target is much larger than startValue (doubling dominates)

sampleTestCases.explanation: double 2 to get 4, then subtract 1 to get 3
subtract 1 from 5 to get 4, then double to get 8
double 3 to get 6, double 6 to get 12, subtract 1 to get 11... a shorter path is double to 6, subtract 1 to 5, double to 10, both take 3 operations

optimal.pattern: reason backward from target: undoing a double is only possible (as integer division) when the number is even, undoing a subtract-1 is always adding 1, so greedily halve whenever possible and add 1 otherwise, until target drops to startValue or below

bruteForce.approach: BFS/DFS forward from startValue, trying both double and subtract-1 at every reachable value, until target is found
bruteForce.time: exponential (unbounded branching forward, since doubling can overshoot arbitrarily)
